Vinkovci Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Vinkovci, Croatia

Not demolished. Vinkovci, built on the site of the Roman city Cibalae (birthplace of emperors Valens and Valentinian I), developed into an important railway junction by 1900 (population 8,500). Jews were barred from settling until 1860, after which migrants from Moravia, Slovakia, and Hungary arrived; businessman Ignatz Gross opened one of the first Jewish retail stores in 1866, and by 1880 the community numbered 272. A first synagogue was built in 1860, replaced by a new one in 1923; Vinkovci hosted the first national rabbinical conference that same year, reflecting the community's significant Zionist and socialist activity. Population peaked at 742 by 1921, still 630 before WWII. Croatian nationalists converted the synagogue to a warehouse in 1942, later burning it; Rabbi M. Frankfurter was tortured and died at Jasenovac. No Jews remained after the war. This cemetery was built in 1870, holding tombstones from 1881 to 1976; its chapel ruins were still visible as of 2009.
